# A single-fiber scaling trap and an exact coordinated deletion

This note addresses whether the strict nonvertex local-depth improvement
can justify reducing the number of positive fibers one at a time. It
cannot do so without an additional global hypothesis. There is an actual
convex source with n=d=1 and FOUR positive fibers (more than 2^n) for which:

* both nonvertex fibers have absolute mixed depth 3/2, compared with
  their ordinary maximal depth 1/2;
* every feasible change of only one actual fiber either leaves the source
  measure unchanged or strictly INCREASES maximal normalized depth;
* a simultaneous change of the two exposed fibers strictly DECREASES
  maximal normalized depth and removes both positive endpoint fibers.

All statements have explicit deterministic centers and matching finite
closed oblique-cap covers. The original depth is 3/8, above OC's 1/4.
Thus this is an obstruction to an unconditional one-fiber surgery rule
or an inference from coordinatewise optimality. It does NOT refute a
surgery theorem using a strict below-OC hypothesis or genuine global
minimality.

## 1. The source and its four-cap certificate

Let C=[0,3] x [0,1], with integer coordinate z and continuous coordinate x.
Its four fibers at z=0,1,2,3 are [0,1], of total mixed mass four. Define

    H_L+ :  x-z/2 >= 0,
    H_L- : -x-z/2+1 >= 0,
    H_R+ :  x+z/2-3/2 >= 0,
    H_R- : -x+z/2-1/2 >= 0.                                (1)

Each cap has mixed mass 3/2. The two left caps cover every point of the
fibers at z=0,1; the two right caps cover every point at z=2,3. Therefore
these four caps cover S and give the global absolute-depth upper bound
3/2 at EVERY candidate.

The three-fiber submeasure on {0,1,2} x [0,1] is centrally symmetric
about (1,1/2), and has mass three. Every ambient closed halfspace containing
this point has mass at least 3/2 on this submeasure: reflection swaps the
two closed through-point halfspaces, whose union is the whole submeasure.
The same argument at (2,1/2) uses {1,2,3} x [0,1]. Thus both points attain
global absolute depth 3/2, and

    beta(C)=3/8.                                            (2)

These centers also show that each nonvertex fiber has local absolute
maximum 3/2. Its own ordinary interval maximum is only 1/2. Hence the
strict local improvement from
`candidate 24ea9b953da308e9` is substantial here.

## 2. Every feasible one-fiber change is an endpoint shrink

Consider any actual convex fiber family obtained by changing just one of
the four interval fibers, while retaining the other three exactly and
introducing no other positive integer fibers. No inclusion of the ambient
bodies needs to be assumed: the required inclusion of their positive
mixed traces follows from the constraints on the changed fiber. Additional
zero-length fibers have zero depth, since their bases are outside the hull
of the positive bases.

If K_1 changes, compatibility with the retained K_0,K_2 gives

    [0,1]=(K_0+K_2)/2 subset K_1.

Compatibility at the retained base 2 gives

    (K_1+K_3)/2 subset K_2=[0,1].

Using 0 and 1 in K_3 shows that every x in K_1 must satisfy 0<=x<=1.
Thus K_1=[0,1]. The same two-sided argument freezes K_2.

If K_0 changes, compatibility at base 1 gives

    (K_0+[0,1])/2 subset [0,1],

which forces K_0 subset [0,1]. The analogous statement holds for K_3.
Thus every nontrivial one-fiber variation is precisely a shrink of an
exposed endpoint interval. Interior deletion is infeasible while the
other fibers remain fixed.

Conversely, every nonempty interval J subset [0,1] is a feasible endpoint
replacement. For example

    C_J=conv( ({0} x J) union ([1,3] x [0,1]) )              (3)

has actual fiber J at 0 and unchanged unit fibers at 1,2,3. Inclusion in
C and retention of the three generating fibers prove their equality;
base 0 is exposed, so its new fiber is exactly J. These are full planar
bodies. A singleton J has zero mixed length at 0, and deleting the base
entirely yields the same positive source measure as the rectangle
[1,3] x [0,1].

## 3. Exact depth throughout every endpoint shrink

Let t=|J| in [0,1], with J in any position inside [0,1], and shrink the
left endpoint as in (3). Its total mixed mass is 3+t. The two left caps
in (1) now have mass t+1/2; the two right caps still have mass 3/2.
All four still cover the changed source, because it is contained in the
original one. This gives absolute maximal depth at most 3/2.

The unchanged symmetric three-fiber submeasure at bases 1,2,3 still gives
absolute depth at least 3/2 at the fixed point (2,1/2). Therefore

    A(C_J)=3/2,
    beta(C_J)=3/[2(3+t)].                                   (4)

This is independent of the location of J. It covers all oblique and
vertical closed caps, including t=0 and any zero-length endpoint point.
The right-endpoint statement follows by z reflection.

For every t<1, (4) is strictly greater than 3/8. Thus an arbitrarily small
nonzero endpoint removal raises normalized maximal depth, and full
one-fiber deletion raises it to 1/2. The absolute optimum has not fallen
at all: the other symmetric core retains an optimal deterministic center.

After any such change, a common continuous affine rescaling to restore
mixed mass four multiplies every cap mass and total mass by the same
factor. It leaves (4) unchanged. Total-mass normalization does not repair
the increase.

## 4. A simultaneous two-endpoint surgery succeeds exactly

For 0<=t<=1, let

    J_t=[(1-t)/2,(1+t)/2],
    K_0(t)=K_3(t)=J_t,    K_1(t)=K_2(t)=[0,1].

These are actual fibers of a convex planar body: interpolate the endpoint
functions linearly between integer bases. The upper function has slopes
(1-t)/2, 0, -(1-t)/2 and is concave; the lower function has the opposite
slopes and is convex. Equivalently take the convex hull of the four
specified generating intervals. Total mixed mass is 2+2t.

All four caps in (1) have mass t+1/2 and still cover the entire source.
For a matching lower bound, retain a symmetric submeasure about
(1,1/2): take J_t at each of the paired bases 0 and 2, and take the full
unit interval at base 1. This submeasure has mass 1+2t, lies in the actual
source, and is centrally symmetric. Thus the fixed candidate (1,1/2)
has absolute depth at least (1+2t)/2. Consequently

    A(t)=t+1/2,
    beta(t)=(1+2t)/[4(1+t)].                                (5)

The derivative with respect to t is 1/[4(1+t)^2]>0. Hence decreasing t
strictly decreases maximal normalized depth throughout the entire
simultaneous path. At t=0 only the two adjacent middle fibers have
positive mixed length, and beta(0)=1/4. The zero-length endpoint points
are actual body points but have zero depth and do not affect the result;
they also remain covered by (1).

Thus the rectangle is a coordinatewise minimum against every feasible
single-fiber replacement, yet is not a global minimum: a two-fiber
variation defeats the trap. This precisely separates the information
supplied by the strict nonvertex gain from the coordinated mass control
still needed in a variational count reduction.

## 5. General exposed-fiber realization and exact scope

The feasibility part of (3) is general. If v is an exposed vertex of the
finite positive base hull and J subset K_v is nonempty compact convex,
then the convex hull of J over v and all other original fibers has exactly
J at v and all the other original positive fibers unchanged. The new hull
is contained in the original one; each retained fiber is a generator;
and a convex representation at exposed v uses only its own generator.
The integer projection introduces no new positive bases. The new hull is
full dimensional when the base hull has full integer affine rank and at
least one other positive full-dimensional fiber remains; otherwise this
assertion is about the exact relative convex fiber hull. At the terminal
collapse to a lower-dimensional J the positive-fiber count decreases.

This is a valid geometric surgery, but (4) proves that its normalized-depth
sign cannot be inferred from inclusion, from the existence of strict local
nonvertex depth gains, or from a subsequent global volume normalization.
The surviving issue is a budget-sensitive coordinated variation at an
actual below-OC global minimizer. This note supplies no substitute for
that hypothesis and makes no claim that such a minimizer exists.

## 6. The same trap with arbitrarily many positive fibers

The phenomenon is not restricted to four fibers. Let m>=2 and start from

    C_m=[0,2m-1] x [0,1],

with 2m positive unit fibers. Put j_L=m-1 and j_R=m. Use the four caps

    x-(z-j_L)-1/2>=0,   -x-(z-j_L)+1/2>=0,
    x+(z-j_R)-1/2>=0,   -x+(z-j_R)+1/2>=0.                  (6)

They cover the left and right sets of integer fibers respectively, and
each has mass m-1/2. The odd block of 2m-1 unit fibers at bases
0,...,2m-2 is centrally symmetric about (m-1,1/2), giving the matching
lower bound. Thus

    A(C_m)=m-1/2,   beta(C_m)=(2m-1)/(4m).                   (7)

Every one-fiber replacement is again an exposed endpoint shrink. Any
interior fiber must contain [0,1] by interpolation of retained fibers on
both sides. If there are two retained consecutive bases on its right,
the same midpoint inclusion used in Section 2 bounds it above by [0,1];
otherwise there are two such bases on its left. The two endpoint fibers
are constrained to lie inside [0,1] by their adjacent two retained bases.

Shrinking one endpoint to any contained interval of length t leaves an
unchanged centrally symmetric odd block of mass 2m-1. The four caps (6)
remain an upper certificate of mass at most m-1/2. Hence exactly

    beta_single(t)=(2m-1)/[2(2m-1+t)].                       (8)

This strictly rises as t decreases from one to zero, ending at one half.
Both deterministic centers and cap signs are unchanged.

Shrinking BOTH endpoints to the same centered interval J_t instead
leaves a symmetric submeasure about (m-1,1/2) consisting of the 2m-3
full fibers at bases 1,...,2m-3 and the two copies of J_t at bases
0 and 2m-2. Its mass is 2m-3+2t. All four caps (6) have exactly half
this mass, so

    beta_pair(t)=(2m-3+2t)/[2(2m-2+2t)].                    (9)

It strictly decreases as t decreases. At t=0 it reaches the value for
the remaining 2m-2 uniform positive fibers. The actual convex realization
uses endpoint widths t and all interior widths one; its upper/lower
endpoint interpolants have the required concavity/convexity. Thus one
fixed pair of exposed fibers can be deleted in this family, while every
single exposed-fiber deletion makes the normalized objective worse.
No corresponding pair-deletion rule is claimed for general convex fibers.
